key_insight: Higher frontline primary care quality was associated with less inappropriate antibiotic receipt and less household antibiotic storage in rural China.
clinical_relevance: Improving primary care quality may support community antibiotic stewardship alongside efforts to address unrestricted antibiotic access.
method: Linked standardized-patient assessments of village doctors to household antibiotic-use data.
Compared ordinary least squares estimates with instrumental-variable double/debiased machine learning estimates.
Used ensemble machine learning to combine multiple provider-level instruments.
evidence_signal: Across approximately 100 rural villages, reported reductions were 6.2 percentage points (OLS) and 9.6 (DML-IV) for inappropriate antibiotic receipt, and 4.1 (OLS) and 10.9 (DML-IV) for household storage.
watch_item: Causal interpretation depends on instrumental-variable assumptions, and findings may not generalize beyond rural Chinese communities.
paper_title: Primary Care Quality and Inappropriate Community Antibiotic Use: Evidence from Linked Provider and Household Data
